content: Circulatory and Gastrointestinal Symptoms A child who is unable to eat or drink, vomits persistently, or shows signs of severe dehydration (such as sunken eyes or very slow skin pinch return) requires immediate medical attention. Severe palmar pallor is another critical sign. Diarrhea accompanied by at least two signs of severe dehydration (lethargy, unconsciousness, sunken eyes, or very slow skin pinch return) is concerning. Signs of shock, such as cold extremities, a capillary refill time exceeding 3 seconds, and a weak, rapid pulse, also warrant urgent care. Any sick child under 2 months of age, or one presenting with a high fever (above 39°C), severe pallor, respiratory distress, or persistent irritability, lethargy, or restlessness, should be stabilized and referred for higher-level care. Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) are particularly vulnerable. Respiratory Symptoms Stridor or oxygen saturation below 90% are serious respiratory concerns. Obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, or central cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin) are critical signs requiring immediate intervention. Neurological Symptoms Seizures, profound lethargy, unconsciousness, neck stiffness, or a bulging fontanelle in infants are indicative of severe neurological conditions. A coma or significantly reduced consciousness level also necessitates urgent medical evaluation. Tuberculosis (TB) Management in Children Children suspected of having TB should be stabilized and referred to higher care if necessary. Once stabilized, they should be evaluated using diagnostic algorithms (Algorithm A or B) to stratify their risk of rapid TB progression. High-risk children include those under 2 years of age, those living with HIV, or those with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). Diagnostic tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used when available. For children with HIV, urine samples should be tested using LF-LAM if accessible. If diagnostic results are positive, TB treatment should begin immediately. If results are unavailable, negative, or delayed, high-risk children should proceed to the next step in the diagnostic algorithm. Diagnostic Algorithms for TB Algorithm A: Used when chest X-rays (CXR) are available. Clinical history, physical examination findings, and CXR results are scored. A score above 10 indicates the need to start TB treatment. Algorithm B: Used when CXR is unavailable. Only clinical history and physical examination findings are scored. A score above 10 also indicates the need for treatment. Risk Factors for Drug-Resistant TB (DR-TB) DR-TB should be suspected in children with contact with a confirmed or presumed DR-TB case, poor response to first-line treatment after 2–3 months, or recurrence of TB after previous treatment. Children with these risk factors should be referred for appropriate care. Diagnostic Tools and Recommendations Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used for bacteriological confirmation of TB and rifampicin resistance. For extrapulmonary TB, appropriate specimens (e.g., lymph node aspirates, pleural fluid, or cerebrospinal fluid) should be collected for testing. In cases of suspected TB meningitis, Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used on cerebrospinal fluid as the initial diagnostic test. For children with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, molecular tests such as low-complexity automated NAATs or line probe assays (LPAs) may be used to detect drug resistance. Treatment Considerations Children with non-severe, drug-susceptible TB are eligible for a shortened 4-month treatment regimen. Non-severe TB includes conditions such as peripheral lymph node TB, uncomplicated pleural effusion, or localized lung disease without cavitation or miliary patterns. Severe TB is characterized by cavitation or bilateral lung disease on CXR. Treatment regimens should be adjusted based on disease severity and drug resistance patterns. Key Messages National TB programs should prioritize bacteriological testing for all children and adolescents suspected of having TB. Rapid diagnostic tools, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra, should be used on various pediatric specimens, including stool, to improve access to testing. Treatment should not be delayed in high-risk groups, even if diagnostic results are pending.
